title: Skydance’s $80 Billion Debt Bomb: How Will Warner Bros. and Paramount’s New Owner Make It Work?
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close On a frigid but bright December morning, David Ellison, his top legal chief Makan Delrahim and coterie of executives took over a subterranean space in the New York City office of investment bank UBS. Just a few dozen feet away, on the other side of the corporate lunch buffet of roast chicken and farro salad, UBS was hosting its Global Media and Communications Conference. Among the speakers on the agenda: Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters, fresh off their deal to buy the Warner Bros. Studio and HBO Max streaming business. Ellison was not on the line up, but he nonetheless took advantage of the location, quietly ushering investors, portfolio managers and analysts into the corner that Paramount secured, where they made their pitch clear: Netflix should not be the home for Warners. We should be. Ellison, one attendee of those meetings told The Hollywood Reporter at the time, was a “man on a mission.” Nearly a year later, Ellison’s mission is complete. In the span of less than a year and a half, he closed deals to secure two of Hollywood’s storied film studios, Paramount and Warner Bros., and brought together two of the industry’s more formidable streaming services in Paramount+ and HBO Max. Ellison, and his consolidated Hollywood giant Skydance , is now an entertainment juggernaut that rivals only Netflix and Disney for scale. Now comes the hard part. The deal is done. The WBD shareholders (and David Zaslav) have been paid, and two companies have become one. What now? The combined company now has the scale of the Netflixes and Disneys of the world, but it also has a debt load big enough ($80 billion!) that there is little room for error, and that debt will need to be serviced sooner rather than later. Services will merge, studios will merge, org structures will be set, the future of CBS News and CNN will be determined, and sports rights will be unified. Streaming prices will likely keep rising (maybe HBO becomes an add-on to Paramount+?), and, yes, more movies will be made, both existing projects like the Days of Thunder sequel and the Game of Thrones film, and new ideas yet to be born. Thousands of layoffs are expected as the companies consolidate, and Ellison and his team are set to lay out the go-forward strategy, with streaming and theatrical films top of mind. Mattel Ynon Kreiz has been tapped to lead Skydance. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images That may be why Ellison persuaded Ynon Kreiz, the CEO of Mattel, to depart the toy giant for a job as co-CEO. When Kreiz, a media veteran (he previously led Maker Studios and Endemol), joined Mattel as its CEO in early 2018, he promised a “transformation” of the company. Just a few months later, he launched an expansive overhaul, slashing 22 percent of its workforce and restructuring it for a tech-forward future. At Paramount, insiders expect him to operate with similar speed, with Ellison and his investors targeting $6 billion in synergies. Kreiz will be the one to lead that effort. “We will embrace the opportunities AI provides to expand what our creatives can imagine and to make our businesses even more productive,” Kreiz and Ellison wrote in a companywide email to staff titled “ Day 1, ” outlining priorities. “The opportunities ahead are enormous, and we intend to seize them. But one principle will never change: technology must serve the art – never the other way around.” RedBird investor Gerry Cardinale will be instrumental in navigating what’s next at Skydance. Giuseppe Maffia/NurPhoto via Getty Images Gerry Cardinale, the founder of RedBird Capital and Ellison’s operating partner in the deal, told a conference last week that the “notion that $6 billion of cost-related synergies means you’re firing all these people is just completely antiquated.” Cardinale insists that much of the cost savings can come from things like combining tech stacks, more efficient marketing spend, and simplifying the vendors it works with.And in their joint letter, Ellison and Kreiz wrote about going “further than traditional synergies. By embracing the most advanced technologies available and embedding them into how we operate, we will work smarter, move faster and unlock efficiencies the merger alone could not deliver.” But everyone knows that significant layoffs are coming as the two companies combine. Paramount, after all, cut about 10 percent of its workforce in 2025 in conjunction with the Skydance deal. “Wake up Hollywood, you’re going to need to rationalize costs,” one industry veteran familiar with leadership’s thinking said. “That’s not a bad thing. That’s called Darwinian evolution.” The real estate footprint of the company will shrink (though the two L.A. studio lots are safe), particularly in New York, where it will have Paramount’s Times Square HQ, the CBS Broadcast Center and Ed Sullivan Theater as well as WBD’s Union Square HQ (home of the Food Network Test Kitchen) as well as CNN’s newsroom and studios in Hudson Yards. According to Bank of America analyst Jessica Reif Ehrlich, the promised savings would “provide a meaningful tailwind to profitability, free cash flow generation and deleveraging over time. “However, history suggests realizing synergies of this magnitude in media is rarely linear, and we anticipate the benefits to be offset by integration costs, execution risk and elevated leverage in the near term,” she continued in a Sep. 24 note. Still, it is likely the only path forward for Skydance. “There’s a virtue to consolidation here, because that is the only way you’re going to level the playing field, and it’s the only way Hollywood is going to put themselves in a position where it balances out the balance of power,” the industry veteran adds, noting the technological disintermediation that threatens Hollywood. “Don’t forget, AI is only valuable with the data that feeds it.” It is also why one of Ellison’s first orders of business was securing the talent of Casey Bloys, the HBO Max chief who will run streaming for the combined company. Going forward, streaming will be the economic engine of the company, and Bloys, who not only shepherded HBO but managed to expand the brand in populist directions via shows like The Pitt and The Penguin , is being given wide leeway to bring that ethos to the combined service. It is an approach that will only become more important once Taylor Sheridan decamps for NBCUniversal in a couple years. An executive at a competing media company said that, among all the executives at Warners, Bloys was the one that they “had to keep.” “If he left, I’m not sure they could have kept HBO intact,” they added. The brand would have existed, of course, but the connective tissue would have been broken. With Pamela Abdy and Mike De Luca on the way out (but James Gunn and Peter Safran still in), the studios will need to stabilize under their new Paramount leadership of Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg. After all, Ellison has promised to release at least 32 movies per year beginning in 2029, and to produce some 170 TV shows. DC, meanwhile, appears to be elevated in the new world order, no longer having to be subservient to the larger WB brand. Skydance’s news leaders: Mark Thompson will continue running CNN while Bari Weiss leads CBS News. And CBS News and CNN remain a particularly hot-button topic, given the chaos that has enveloped CBS since Ellison appointed Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief. Ellison is said to genuinely admire Weiss and her vision, which is premised on appealing to a silent majority of Americans who are not far left or far right, and being somewhat contrarian or against the grain. “She operates with the idea that if every other place is taking one approach or angle to a story, there might be room to do something different, even if the underlying facts are the facts,” one TV news veteran said. But it is far from obvious that she will get any oversight over CNN, in fact one executive at a competing news operation said that it would be “crazy” to do so. That is why the official news that Thompson had inked a deal to remain chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN such a relief to veterans of the news brand. The issue is that, while CBS News is seen as a breakeven or barely profitable endeavor, one primarily about brand-building, CNN is an actual profit center. CNN is projected to have $1.8 billion in revenue in 2026, according to disclosures from Warner Bros. Discovery, rising to $1.9 billion in 2027, $2 billion in 2028 and $2.2 billion by 2030. CNN’s adjusted EBITDA in 2026 is estimated to be about $600 million, before falling to $500 million in 2027 and remaining flat at $600 million through 2030. While CNN’s revenue is relatively modest compared to the rest of the WBD cable portfolio ($9.9 billion in 2026) its EBITDA is strong, with every other channel in its portfolio combining for $3.8 billion and expected to fall to $1.9 billion through 2030. CNN, by contrast, is expected to be flat in EBITDA in that same period. But there will be challenges. Given the debt load, the combined company will need to keep those profits flowing, and combining CBS News and CNN is seen as an obvious source of cost savings, but it is not clear how that can happen with both Weiss and Thompson in the building. And all eyes will be on CNN’s editorial independence board: Who will be on it, what power they will have, and if it salves concerns from viewers and politicos. George Cheeks will become, for all intents and purposes, the most powerful executive in linear TV. His purview will include CBS, and more cable channels than any other company by far, spanning sports, entertainment, news and more. But most observers recognize that those channels will be milked for cash, with wide cuts expected as the company seeks to harvest the revenue from carriage fees and redistribute to other priorities, like streaming, and paying down that pesky debt. CBS Sports will become a juggernaut, with the NFL, all of March Madness, college football, MLB, NHL, UFC, The Masters, international soccer rights and much more. JB Perrette, a WBD holdover, will be responsible for the business of TV and streaming, letting Bloys and Cheeks cook on content, balancing declining linear TV and growing streaming. And the company will also have what an executive at a competitor called a “secret weapon”: Warner Bros. Games. The game studio is the home of Mortal Kombat , and has produced hit games based on IP like Batman , Harry Potter and Game of Thrones . Earlier this year Ellison launched a new gaming studio within Paramount, and the combined game studio will be formidable, with a vast library of IP to mine (including from outside partners like Disney, which has worked with both studios). While all eyes will be on the film and TV output, the competing executive speculated that the game studio could become a bigger part of the business than Hollywood expects. Still, as Morgan Stanley’s Sean Diffley noted Sep. 22, this is ultimately about creating an intellectual property behemoth that only has one true rival in Disney (Netflix and YouTube are streaming giants, but not IP giants). “While in many ways the hard part begins now (and we are fully sympathetic to the complexity of integrating large media assets), the risk of not getting the asset was significantly greater and we believe scale and IP are important in an ever increasingly fragmented media ecosystem,” Diffley wrote. But first, they have that $80 billion in debt to reduce. House of brands: All of the studios, channels and assets in the combined Skydance empire. THR

title: Skydance CEOs Acknowledge Layoffs Will Be Coming After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: Read the Full Memo
full_text: Breaking News Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes Oct 6, 2026 8:32am PT Skydance CEOs Acknowledge Layoffs Will Be Coming After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: Read the Full Memo David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz say there will be 'difficult decisions that affect our workforce' By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Skydance CEOs Acknowledge Layoffs Will Be Coming After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger: Read the Full Memo 16 minutes ago Paramount-Warner Bros. $111 Billion Merger Officially Closes: ‘Today Is a Historic Day, Not Just for Skydance but for Our Entire Industry,’ David Ellison Says 3 hours ago David Zaslav Bids Farewell to Warner Bros. Employees in Video on Eve of Skydance Merger Close: ‘It’s Been a Great Honor to Be Alongside All of You’ 20 hours ago See All Getty Images Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery have officially merged into Skydance Corp. And the top leaders have notified the new company’s staffers that layoffs are in the offing. David Ellison , chairman and CEO, and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz (formerly chief exec of Mattel) sent a memo to employees at the combined company Tuesday morning around 9:40 a.m. ET after the deal closed outlining the operating philosophy of Skydance — and its goals in the years ahead. Related Stories Casey Bloys Poised to Run HBO and Paramount+ as Cindy Holland Confirms Her Exit From Studio on Eve of Merger Closing Paramount, Warner Bros. Insiders Were Stunned by the Settlement With State AGs. Now They're Girding for Inevitable Mass Layoffs The duo acknowledged that layoffs will be part of the process in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by Variety . “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce,” the execs wrote. “We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully.” Popular on Variety Paramount execs have said they are shooting to achieve more than $6 billion in annualized cost savings over three years — and part of that will come from layoffs. The company has not revealed at this point the extent of the job cuts it expects. According to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August, the merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone. However, overall, Ellison and Kreiz sounded an upbeat note, telling the troops that together they will “build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology. The goal was never simply to add more production capacity, brands or IP. It was to unite the talent, resources and capabilities of these companies into a stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry.” “Together, we will give these iconic studios the opportunity to win for generations to come,” the execs wrote in the 1,705-word memo, which has the subject line “Day 1.” Here’s the full memo: Team, Today we begin an exciting new chapter as Skydance. Getting here has been quite a journey. Over the past year and beyond, it has taken hard work, perseverance and commitment with many challenges along the way – but we did it! To everyone at both companies who helped get us to this moment: thank you. Thank you for your patience, your resilience and, above all, your belief in what we could accomplish together. Bringing Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery together fulfills a vision that began with Skydance’s acquisition of Paramount: to build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology. The goal was never simply to add more production capacity, brands or IP. It was to unite the talent, resources and capabilities of these companies into a stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry. Together, we will give these iconic studios the opportunity to win for generations to come. Built for What’s Ahead As all of you know, our industry is in a period of profound change. Audiences have more choices than ever, technology is reshaping how stories are created, distributed and experienced, and competition for people’s time and attention has never been greater. We don’t just want to succeed in this environment – we want to win and help shape the future of the industry. We want to lead. And that starts with what we’re building together: a company that tells great stories in every genre, for audiences everywhere, on every platform. A company that can compete in a crowded market and win at global scale, create enduring value for all stakeholders, and strengthen the industry as a whole. As owner-operators, we’re in this for the long term, committed to building Skydance for the future – not simply optimizing for the next quarter or the next year, but creating a company built to endure, evolve and remain relevant. That means being creative-first, audience-focused, tech-forward and globally scaled – building a thriving ecosystem where stories and worlds are imagined, brought to life and experienced by audiences of all ages, everywhere. At the center of it all is a clear purpose: to entertain, inspire and inform the world through extraordinary storytelling. And we’ll be guided every step of the way by shared priorities that shape how we intend to operate, how we make decisions, how we work together and how we show up for our audiences, our partners and one another. Our Top Priorities To bring that mission to life, these are the priority areas where we will concentrate our energy: Win in Storytelling Great stories remain at the heart of everything we do. We will invest in the ideas, creators, franchises and experiences that captivate audiences around the world and create lasting cultural impact. On the big screen, we are committed to making at least 30 movies a year, pairing original stories from today’s most exciting filmmakers with beloved franchises like Harry Potter, Mission: Impossible, The Lord of the Rings, DC, Transformers and Star Trek. On television and streaming, it means storytelling like Game of Thrones, Landman, NCIS, Tracker and SpongeBob SquarePants. In games, it means worlds like Hogwarts Legacy and Mortal Kombat; and in live sports, it means the NFL on CBS, the UFC, UEFA and March Madness, just to name a few. Become the Most Technologically Capable Media Company Technology is fundamentally reshaping our industry, and we intend to be at the forefront. We will use technology, data and emerging capabilities to improve how we create, distribute and monetize content, from new production tools to personalization and entirely new ways for fans to engage with the stories they love. We will embrace the opportunities AI provides to expand what our creatives can imagine and to make our businesses even more productive. The opportunities ahead are enormous, and we intend to seize them. But one principle will never change: technology must serve the art – never the other way around. Lead in a Crowded Market We came together to create another major competitor in the industry. And with our combined scale, assets and global reach, we are positioned to take on some of the largest technology and media companies in the world and to lead in an evolving entertainment landscape. We will use that strength to drive synergies, operate with discipline and invest in the long-term growth of our business. And we will go further than traditional synergies. By embracing the most advanced technologies available and embedding them into how we operate, we will work smarter, move faster and unlock efficiencies the merger alone could not deliver. Earn Trust Every Day Trust is foundational to everything we do. And we are committed to earning it every day by communicating directly, following through on our commitments and listening closely to those we serve and work alongside. That is essential to our reputation and our long-term success. As we work toward these goals, we must never lose sight of what matters most: our people. We will build a culture where people feel respected, empowered, supported and proud of the work they do. And we will extend that same commitment, with reliability and responsibility, to our creators, audiences, consumers, advertisers and partners. None of what we accomplish happens in a vacuum. It reflects everyone joining forces to unlock the full potential of our assets: an unmatched portfolio of brands, franchises, libraries, IP and creative talent, with decades of history and, in many cases, decades of opportunity still ahead. Together, we can reach audiences across platforms, markets, and generations in ways neither Paramount nor WBD could have achieved alone. With the talent, scale, relationships and resources to build on, we can create something truly distinctive. For audiences, it means more choice and more ways to experience the stories they love. For creators, it means a partner with the scale and capabilities to help their best ideas reach the widest possible audience. For our partners, it means a broader, more powerful platform to build on. And for the broader creative community, it means an enduring commitment to storytelling and the people who make it possible. That is the foundation of Skydance. And it’s why this combination matters so much. Honoring an Extraordinary Legacy The union of these two iconic companies represents an exciting future. But, just as important as what we build together is preserving what has made them iconic in the first place. Paramount and Warner Bros. each have a distinct identity and extraordinary legacy that deserves to stand on its own. In choosing our corporate brand, we never wanted to diminish, alter or overshadow any of the assets that have global recognition and have withstood the test of time. Both studios will continue to operate under their own names, and audiences will still see the Paramount mountain and the Warner Bros. shield before the films and shows they love. Warner Bros. is woven into the history of modern entertainment, from film and television to journalism, sports, unscripted programming and some of the world’s most recognizable characters and franchises. Paramount has an equally extraordinary legacy, with more than a century of storytelling that helped define the American film industry and shape entertainment across every medium. We realized early on that simply combining the two names – WarnerParamount, ParaWarner or ParamountWarner – accomplished none of what we wanted. Every variation somehow made two giants feel smaller, not greater. It asked each to give something up rather than allowing us to create something new. This isn’t a merger of convenience. It’s the beginning of a new era in entertainment, and we wanted a name that looks forward rather than one that simply splices together the past. That brought us to Skydance – a name that obviously has special meaning to David, who chose it for his own studio 20 years ago. It evokes possibility: scale and ambition, creativity and imagination, artistry and innovation. Most importantly, it doesn’t compete with either legacy. It gives the new company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. – and all our extraordinary brands – to remain in the spotlight. Because ultimately, what we are bringing together is much more than brands and libraries. It is the creative spirit, ambition and craftsmanship that have kept these companies culturally relevant for generations. That spirit will continue to be a core part of who we are at Skydance. And who we are will also be defined by what we strive to accomplish – not just for our company, but for the industry at large. That means looking ahead to the forces that are reshaping entertainment and finding ways to harness them to expand what’s possible – for creators, for audiences and for the business itself. Financial Strength We’re building a diversified company with the financial strength to compete aggressively and the discipline to create sustainable value. That’s not just important to our investors – it’s important to all of us. A financially strong, well-run company gives us the freedom to take creative risks, invest in our people and our technology, and pursue the kind of opportunities that set us apart. In concrete terms, we are together one of the largest media and entertainment companies in the world, with nearly $70 billion in revenue. As we have said publicly, we are also targeting at least $6 billion in synergies, which will make us leaner and more nimble and free up capital to invest in the stories, creators and technology that matter most. Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce. We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully. The Road Ahead Today is Day One. We have an incredible collection of assets. Extraordinary creative talent. Global scale. The technology to lead. And most important, we have the people who bring it all to life every day. We have everything we need to win, and that is our goal: to build a next-generation global media and entertainment company that puts audiences first, empowers creators, embraces innovation and creates lasting value for generations to come. But none of this happens without you. Thank you for everything you’ve brought to this moment. We’re proud to write this next chapter with you. Now the real work begins. Let’s go! title: Steven Spielberg Returns to ‘Transformers’ Franchise, Michael Bay in Talks to Direct for Paramount
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 6, 2026 8:30am Mark Wahlberg in 'Transformers: Age of Extinction.' Industrial Light & Magic/Paramount Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Steven Spielberg is returning to Paramount ’s cult Transformers franchise alongside longtime producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura and with Michael Bay, long a master of mayhem, in talks to possibly direct the next tentpole for fanboys of vehicles. Spielberg will focus on all creative aspects of the next live-action film based on a Hasbro line of toys. He will also executive produce the eighth live-action installment as Paramount looks to build out the Transformers universe. Bay directed the first five films in the Transformers franchise as he and his team of creators allowed the titans and other techno-creatures to clash amid action sequences spectacularly conceived and executed. Related Stories Business Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant TV 'East of Eden' Star Mike Faist on Male Ego, Love Triangles and Still Learning from Steven Spielberg Bay directed Transformers (2007), Revenge of the Fallen (2009), Dark of the Moon (2011), Age of Extinction (2014) and The Last Knight (2017). Travis Knight helmed the 2018, 1980s-set prequel Bumblebee . It’s understood Transformers headliner Shia LaBeouf will not return for the eighth installment, and there’s no word on a storyline and other possible casting. LaBeouf played a young Sam Witwicky, a teenager who bought his first car but never expected it to come to life, in the first Transformers movie, and returned for sequels. Spielberg met with Paramount Pictures co-chairs Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg in August 2025, ahead of the studio having now completed a merger with Warner Bros Discovery. Transformers 8 will be based on a script set in the modern day by Jason Fuchs, with Di Bonventura helping develop and Spielberg reading and signing off. Spielberg held creative roles for the first two Transformers films that launched the franchise and generated over $5.4 billion in global box office revenue as Hasbro’s toy brand gained a worldwide following. Di Bonaventura, Mark Vahradian, Don Murphy, Tom DeSanto and Hasbro will produce. THR

title: Sam Bankman-Fried Docuseries Set at Amazon (Exclusive)

Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 6, 2026 8:30am Sam Bankman-Fried. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Logo text Amazon is getting into the crypto game, kind of, though it may have picked the wrong partner. Propagate and Amazon MGM Studios have teamed on the three-part Sam Bankman-Fried documentary series The Boy Who Stole Billions? , which is set for a November release, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. The question mark in the title is doing some serious work here. The Boy Who Stole Billions ? gained access to Bankman-Fried in prison, so you’ll get his side of the story straight from the fraud’s horse’s mouth. The docuseries “delves into one of the biggest frauds in U.S. history with unprecedented access and exclusive firsthand accounts from Sam Bankman-Fried himself from prison,” according to Prime Video . Related Stories TV Emmy Awards Enter Streaming Era: Prime Video, TV Academy Ink Six-Year Deal Lifestyle Prime Big Deal Days 2026: What to Snag (and Skip) During Amazon's 48-Hour Sale It continued: “At 30, Sam Bankman-Fried ran a $32 billion crypto empire until he was convicted of stealing $8 billion in customer funds, one of the biggest frauds in U.S. history. For the first time, he tells his story from prison in this riveting three-part docuseries. Was it fraud, or did his risky bets simply spiral out of control? With never before seen interviews from those who built FTX with him, the series probes SBF’s pressure-cooker world, inner circle, and complicated relationship with his CEO and former girlfriend, Caroline Ellison.” FTX was a major cryptocurrency exchange. It collapsed in November 2022 due to severe fund mismanagement, a massive multi-billion-dollar deficit and, depending who you ask, fraud. Bankman-Fried was in Ben MacKenzie’s ( The O.C. ) crypto-takedown documentary Everyone Is Lying to You for Money (2025). In 2023, he appeared on 60 Minutes in segment “The Rise and Fall of Sam Bankman-Fried.” The Boy Who Stole Billions? is produced by Amazon MGM Studios, Propagate and West Buttermilk with Howard T. Owens, Ben Silverman, Drew Buckley, Isabel San Vargas, Taylor Levin, Nanette Burstein and James Packer serving as executive producers. THR

title: Inside the Shocking Decision to End ‘Young Sheldon’ at Its Peak (Exclusive Excerpt)
full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close Sheldon (Iain Armitage) on 'Young Sheldon.' Sonja Flemming/CBS Logo text “One thing about a television show that succeeds is that a family is created over many years, and when you bring it to an end, there’s grieving,“ Chuck Lorre reflected on the ending of CBS hit show Young Sheldon . The series, which premiered in 2017 and starred Iain Armitage, Lance Barber, Raegan Revord, Zoe Perry, Annie Potts, Montana Jordan and Emily Osment, ended in 2024 after seven seasons. And though Young Sheldon was successful, in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic and joint writers and actors strikes in 2023, it became apparent to the show’s creative team that the narrative of the TV show‘s story was leading to an end. Related Stories TV Harlan Coben Previews 'Final Twist' Season 2, "Bonkers" First Episode and How His Onscreen Work Has Evolved General News Joey and Matthew Lawrence on Launching Their New Graphic Novel, '90s Nostalgia and Hopes for an Animated Series Jessica Radloff, New York Times best-selling author and host of The Official Big Bang Theory Podcast for HBO Max and Warner Bros., explores the decision to end the show and more in her upcoming book, Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy , releasing on Oct. 20 from Grand Central Publishing. Through exclusive interviews, Radloff offers behind-the-scenes revelations and heartfelt anecdotes from the show‘s cast and crew as well as the emotional journey that led to the end of the series. Though any end to a show can be bittersweet, Radloff‘s book explores how the cast experienced an array of emotions after learning the show would not be continuing — while on a Zoom call. Four days after the actors’ strike ended, castmembers Barber, Perry, Potts, Armitage, Revord, Jordan and Osment were invited to a mandatory Zoom meeting with Lorre, Steve Molaro and Steve Holland where they would shockingly learn the show‘s fate. Below, The Hollywood Reporter shares an excerpt on the Zoom call that ended it all from Radloff‘s Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy . ***** The spring of 2023 marked the start of a complicated time. Young Sheldon had just wrapped season six and had one more year on a three-season renewal that began in 2021. If Young Sheldon was going to continue past season seven, the main cast would have to negotiate new contracts. The goal is always the same when you’re on a hugely successful show: Get more money. But times were changing in Hollywood, and budgets were starting to shrink post-pandemic. Then there was the fact that Iain Armitage and Raegan Revord were getting older. Time on the show had already been slowed down since it was established that George dies when the twins are 14, so at one point do you totally abandon Big Bang canon? And if you don’t, do you continue a show without the gigantic presence that is and was George Cooper? As if the writers and producers didn’t have enough to think about, a writers’ strike was looming, which had the potential to bring Hollywood to a halt. But if the pandemic taught anyone anything, it’s that you have to take each day as it comes. And so, when the last episode of season six was completed, Lorre, Molaro, and Holland approached the upcoming summer hiatus with the hope that they’d be back in the writers room come June, back in production in late July and on the air in September. Steve Holland: You get to the end of a season, and you’re exhausted and burned out, so the thought of “Let’s start planning for season seven in case there is a writer’s strike” was not really something that was really feasible. Plus, writing that early wouldn’t have really helped anyway, as it takes about six weeks of writing and brainstorming to even get to the point of planning a new season and the first few episodes. And while we did think a strike was likely, we also didn’t think it was going to last that long. Nor did anyone else. But on May 2, 2023, the Writers Guild of America officially went on strike due to labor disputes with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers. Nearly two and a half months later, on July 14, 2023, the Screen Actors Guild followed suit. At this point, even if the writers’ strike had been resolved, writing teams would already have been behind schedule for their normal September premieres. Grand Central Publishing Lance Barber: My concern was for the future of the business and everybody’s career, which is still playing out. We made strides, but work is so limited in this town. At the time, though, I felt like we were one of the shows that was earning revenue since we were a primetime hit show. But we were all on the picket lines, for sure. Nobody wanted to see a strike happen — and I’ll speak for myself — but I could afford to be on strike, which is not the situation for most actors. And so that wasn’t lost on me that I could fight the good fight because I could afford to. Holly Revord: During the strike, we were with Holland a lot, picketing. We didn’t know what the future of Young Sheldon looked like, but I was always trying to have conversations with Holland about it, like what happens after George dies, and Mary’s a single mom to teenagers. Lance Barber: I think from what I was told secondhand, the producers said, “Yeah, we want to see Missy graduate high school, and we want to take this as long as we can and we can cheat [the timeline].” Iain Armitage: I didn’t expect the show to go on forever. I expected it to go for about six or seven years. Lee Armitage: But I think Raegan felt they were promised like, “You’re going to be doing this show until…“ and Iain never had that conversation. People would say, “Would you do more?” just to find out where he was with it. And I would tell Iain, “Don’t give a yes or a no; take the time to think it through, and talk to your agent, talk to me, think about it.” So all my care was put into how to handle it if that ever came about. Raegan Revord: I definitely thought we had another couple years. At some point, I think business affairs came to us to negotiate about a pickup, so when we were told the show was ending, it was shocking. And yeah, Lance, Zoe and I would be surrounding Holland all the time on the picket line, pitching stories, asking what might happen, et cetera. We definitely asked a lot of questions, but I do know everything was tentative because in this business, nothing is concrete until the episode is out. Still, there were discussions about where the show could go after George’s death, but we weren’t ever told, like, “Oh yeah, it’s happening.” That was never told. But the discussions were there. Steve Holland: The actors joined us a bunch on the picket lines and there was definitely—and understandably—a lot of interest about the future of the show. At that time, we weren’t even sure we were going to get back to doing a season seven or if the strike was going to throw the whole season off. But I certainly never thought the show had four more years left in it. After 148 days, the writers’ strike officially ended on September 27, 2023. While the writers were now free to go back to work, the actors were still on strike. Steve Holland: The fear of the writers’ and actors’ strike was the longer it went on, the smaller you saw season seven becoming. We wanted to make sure we could give it what it deserved if it was going to be our final season, but as the actors’ strike dragged on into the fall, our hope for 22 episodes became 18 episodes, then 16 episodes. We knew basically in season seven that George was going to die, and Sheldon was going to go away to Caltech. Steve Molaro: We held off on those big moments in show time for as long as we could. But we were now approaching them, and I didn’t want to make a show without George and with the main character away at grad school. Steve Holland: Steve was very adamant that he didn’t want to do another season of Young Sheldon after that. I think I agreed with him, but I was more open to seeing what a season eight would look like. Steve Molaro: They could have gone on. There’s a world where there could have been a season eight, and I could have just said, “I wish you all well; I’m going to take a step away from this.” And I would have. I personally did not want to make the show without George. So if everybody wanted it and were excited to do it and had a take on it that they were psyched about, I would have probably consulted, but I was ready to take a step back and think about other things. Steve Holland: Molaro and I sat down at Chuck’s house and chatted about whether there was a world beyond George dying and Sheldon going away. And as we were talking about it, it felt like the story arc that was Young Sheldon was really so much about Sheldon looking back on his relationship specifically with his dad, and realizing and seeing it as a dad in a different light. That wasn’t the thesis statement going in, but as the show went on, it became very clear that the emotional through line was an older Sheldon with kids looking back on his parents, but specifically his dad, and realizing that he had maybe been unfair to him for most of his life. And it felt like that was the end of that show. It also felt like coming back to it without Sheldon there or George there … it would be hard to just to not live in the grief of George being gone. It felt like it was going to be going past the end of the story. Chuck Lorre: I absolutely agreed that we told the story, and once season seven was finished, Young Sheldon had come to an end. Sheldon was now taller than most of the other characters on the show, so the “young” word was kind of looking a little silly. Steve Molaro: Plus, we were not going to go follow Sheldon to Caltech. That was already a show, and it’s called The Big Bang Theory . And I’m not interested in telling the stories in the years before he met Leonard. But based on the ratings, I understand why a season eight on paper would have made sense. I just didn’t think creatively it was a good choice. What Molaro and Holland did think was a good choice was a possible spin-off focusing on Georgie, his wife Mandy, and their new baby, CeeCee. It wasn’t until after the writers’ strike ended that the two started putting more thought into the idea, but the seed was actually planted a year before. Alex Reid: We were on location in season six doing something with Georgie and Mandy, and it was going smoothly and all the jokes were landing. I just happened to be standing there when Molaro said something to Holland and the writers, like, “I could see myself doing five years with these two.” There was always talk or whispers of a spin-off, so at that point, he wasn’t saying that for nothing. Steve Holland: I think it became clear watching Georgie and Mandy together that they were great, and to follow them would be great. What we didn’t know at that point was when that would be. We didn’t know how long Young Sheldon was going to go. Montana Jordan, Emily Osment and Iain Armitage in Young Sheldon . Bill Inoshita/2024 Warner Bros. Entertainment That is until late September 2023, when Molaro and Holland decided to actually present the idea of a Georgie and Mandy spin-off to Lorre, knowing that there would be no season eight of Young Sheldon. Steve Molaro: I called Chuck and said, “Here’s my pitch: we make a show for Georgie and Mandy living with her parents, who we already know and love, but we flip it back to multi-cam.” There was a pause, then Chuck said, “You son of a bitch! Stop getting me excited to do multi-cam again!” He loved it. Chuck Lorre: It made perfect sense. It just felt right. Steve Molaro: We knew that CBS wanted Young Sheldon to keep going, regardless of what the creative was, but we had found this other path where we could potentially keep something going that was related to it but without having the weight of George gone, and Sheldon gone. There wasn’t any joy in that, but by flipping the format to multi-cam and focusing on other aspects seemed to me to be a version where if they wanted to do that, we could keep the comedy and joy going. Alex Reid: Molaro also found the single-camera process completely tedious and frustrating. He could do another single-cam if it was eight episodes, but he can’t do six or seven seasons of 22 episodes a season. It just wore him down. He loved how the episodes turned out, and was very proud of them, but how the sausage was made was really not appealing to him. But the window to bring Young Sheldon to a close with enough episodes to tell that story was getting narrower as the actors’ strike went on. Plus, as soon as the actors’ strike ended, CBS was going to enter into negotiations with the actors since their contracts would be expiring soon anyway. Steve Holland: It was still a big hit, and it’s tricky because financially, things get more expensive as they go on, and if we had done another season of Young Sheldon , they might have had to cut the budget some to do it. Who knows? The shows get more expensive and the return on them gets less. They’re already presold into syndication, so each show that you make becomes less and less valuable at a certain point. So there’s a world where CBS would have said yes to more seasons, but cut the budget for it, and we also weren’t interested in doing a slightly slashed version of the show. So we met with the studio (Warner Bros. Television) and network (CBS) to talk about Young Sheldon , and I think they were probably assuming we were going to talk about season eight. Instead, we told them this was going to be the last season, but we had some good news. I had a picture of Montana and Emily holding the baby on my iPad, and we said, “But we have another show for you, and it’s this one here.” To their credit, they were incredibly supportive, but I think in that moment they were incredibly taken aback because they were not expecting us to say we want to end the biggest comedy on television right now. Connor Kilpatrick: I didn’t think CBS was going to let it be the end, truly. That might have been wishful thinking, but I know they didn’t want it to end. I had always heard the story of when Charlie Sheen left Two and a Half Men , Chuck wanted to end the show, and Les Moonves (then chairman and CEO of CBS) told him something like, “I don’t care if you’re a part of it, but there will be a Two and a Half Men on CBS.” [ Author’s note: And there was, with Sheen being replaced by Ashton Kutcher.] So I had a feeling that CBS was going to be like, “We don’t care if you guys walk away, but we’re going to keep making Young Sheldon .” Iain Armitage in Young Sheldon . Bill Inoshita / 2024 Warner Bros. Entertainment Inc. But that’s not what happened. Given Lorre, Molaro and Holland’s success with The Big Bang Theory and Young Sheldon , CBS trusted their creative instincts and had faith in a potential spin-off. The only problem was that since the actors’ strike was still ongoing, Lorre, Molaro and Holland couldn’t approach Montana Jordan or Emily Osment to even see if they were interested. Steve Holland: We assumed they would all want to do it, but honestly, the one question mark was Montana, because he and [his now wife] Jenna were having a baby. I really didn’t know him well enough to know whether he wanted to keep doing this or go back to Texas, because he really loves being in Texas, and he loves being around his family. I could have seen a world where he was like, “I’ve got my Young Sheldon money and this has been great, but I just want to go back to Texas and raise my baby.” And then we would have no show. We just didn’t know. And we couldn’t ask him at that moment because they were still on strike. Eventually the actors’ strike would come to an end, and on Nov. 9, 2023, 118 days after it began, the work stoppage was over. The cast of Young Sheldon was excited to get back to work but had no idea about the decisions that were already made behind the scenes. Steve Holland: We had to do two things back to back, which was unfortunate, because we were about to start production. We had to inform the cast and tell them this was going to be the last season. We had done it on Big Bang , which was worse, but at least that was in person. In this case, because many of them were out of town due to the strikes, we had to get them all on Zoom. We wanted to tell them as soon as possible because we felt they should know, and didn’t want the news to leak. On top of that, we couldn’t talk to Montana and Emily about the spin-off until we told everybody about Young Sheldon ending, because we didn’t want them to be the only ones who knew this was going to be the last season of Young Sheldon . That didn’t feel fair to them. And so, four days after the actors’ strike had ended, Lance Barber, Zoe Perry, Annie Potts, Iain Armitage, Raegan Revord, Montana Jordan, and Emily Osment received invites to a mandatory Zoom meeting with Chuck Lorre, Steve Molaro and Steve Holland. Lee Armitage: When I got the hint that there might be something more to this meeting, I made it my business to know for Iain. I don’t want anybody sort of timing a surprise, good or bad, like that. I know what’s on his mind, and I know what he needs to know when. And so I found out. I don’t think they handled it perfectly, and I also think there’s no perfect way to handle it. Iain Armitage: I was lucky, because I was not blindsided by their announcement when they told us. Holly Revord: I knew it wasn’t good news because Chuck was also going to be on the Zoom, and Chuck can’t make the decision alone to do more seasons. They would have had to reach out to everyone’s representatives, and then the cast would have to decide to do more or not. So I knew there was a decision made for us, and especially when the email invite said, “Meeting with Chuck tomorrow … you have to be there.” I think we asked if the kids had to be there, and they said yes, which meant that if they were in the middle of schooling, we’d have to get them out of a lesson. Plus, no one’s agent had come to talk to us. So we knew. I didn’t want Raegan to be blindsided, but I didn’t want to tell them either. So I just said, “This is either really good news or really bad news.” Raegan said, “Okay,” but I don’t think they really thought much of it. The show was still doing so well in the ratings, and we were hearing from Warner Bros. business affairs there might be a multiple-season pickup, so in Raegan’s brain, the show was going to keep going. Annie Potts: We were the number one show on network TV. So when they scheduled a Zoom meeting, I thought they were going to say, “Listen, we got a pickup for three years!” Perry and Barber, meanwhile, were less optimistic. Zoe Perry: There was a lot of uncertainty, but once we heard there was a Zoom, I thought, “Okay, this is it, because you wouldn’t normally have a meeting like that.” Lance Barber: I assumed it might be to announce the end, because otherwise they would have to negotiate new contracts and they knew everybody would hold out and go to the table for some big money. But the show already had a natural stopping point coming up that would be appropriate, storytelling-wise. If they continued it, which they did in another way, it would be one that behooved them business wise. So I kind of felt from that three-season pickup at the end of season four that that was where it was headed. But I hoped for myself and everybody else that it would bring us work for longer. On Tuesday, Nov. 14, 2023, the cast logged on for the Zoom meeting and made small talk with each other. Everyone was in a good mood, if a little nervous about what was going to be discussed. There was some teasing about Lance Barber’s beard, followed by everyone congratulating Montana Jordan on the news that he was going to be a dad. “Our baby’s all grown up,” Zoe Perry could be heard saying, with Barber joking he was sick of his real family and ready to be reunited with his TV family on set. Once Chuck Lorre logged on, Steve Holland began by saying, “Hello everybody, it’s so nice to see your faces. And I know some of you have guessed this, but we wanted to get everyone in one place to make it official that this is going to be the final season of Young Sheldon .” He paused, and everyone remained quiet, but their feelings were written all over their faces. A second or two later, he continued: “[This] is incredibly difficult to say because of what an amazing place it is to work, and a lot of that is due to all of you. So thank all of you for being such incredible partners, and friends, and castmates, and family on this run.” Steve Holland: I said, “To us, this just feels like the natural end of the show,” and “We talked about whether there was a version going forward, but this just felt that it was the right time to end it and go out on top.” But there was a lot of frustration and anger on that Zoom, like, we’re still a big hit show, and who walks away from that? Our feeling was, that’s when you walk away, when it’s still great, and don’t let it sort of taper off into mediocrity. But it’s a lot to drop on people. And especially for the kids and their parents, this had been such a huge chunk of their lives. I mean, it’s scary. It was scary for the Big Bang cast, knowing that was ending, but when you’re now 15 or 16, and you’ve been on this show for eight years, it’s what you know. And you’re losing a family. It’s a lot to process. Steve Molaro: It was tough. We’re all a family and we all care about each other. I don’t want to watch anybody be sad or be shocked, but at the end of the day, I still believe creatively, that was the right time to end that story. Steve and I feel the same way about how Big Bang ended. They wanted it to keep going, and yes, there’s a world where it could have, and I’m only speaking from a creative standpoint, but creatively, to us, it’s hard for me to imagine a version of that that wouldn’t have been challenging. Montana Jordan was the first to speak once Holland finished relaying the news. “Well, I wasn’t expectin’ that!” he said, his voice choking up. There was some uneasy laughter, and then, what everyone else was too afraid to say came from the only person who could. Annie Potts: I said, “Well, that sucks! I don’t like that at all!” I felt I had voiced what everybody else was feeling, and I thought, “Well, I shot myself in the foot.” I went full Meemaw on them, I have to say. I mean, what did they think we were going to do? It wasn’t couched in “We know this is going to be upsetting,” so we had a second to collect or read what was happening in that Zoom room. I felt like I had been thunderstruck or lightning struck. It was more than a rumble. It was a direct hit. Holly Revord: I wish we could have all been together. [ Tearing up ] It would have been nice in those moments to hug each other. And especially for Raegan, who literally didn’t say one thing on the call; they were mute. I will never forget Annie’s reaction. I wanted to be in person to hug her because she broke my heart. Montana Jordan: I was in Texas, and just sat there, shocked. I kinda wish they had done it in person because then you can show your love to them, but I understand their reasons. I was just kinda sittin’ there in my own thoughts, like, “Oh, did he just say that?” And then right after, I called Jenna and said, “I better start applying to McDonald’s or something.” Steve Holland: Montana seemed really shocked and upset about Young Sheldon ending, so I immediately thought, “Oh, he’s going to do the spin-off [now based on that reaction].” Montana Jordan and Emily Osment in Young Sheldon . Sonja Flemming/CBS Emily Osment, unaware that she’d be receiving good news soon thereafter, said, “I just got here! This is awful. You guys have been here so much longer than me. That sucks.” Molaro and Holland took a moment to then reiterate that this wouldn’t be so hard if they didn’t all truly enjoy each other, followed by Lorre announcing that the upcoming final season would consist of 14 episodes (shortened because of the length of the strikes), whereas most other shows were only doing 10. Lance Barber: Young Sheldon could have gone on as The Cooper Family , but it still would lack some of the integrity of the show, potentially, if it moved beyond that storyline. So I was grateful, as I was from the beginning, to have the story end there because of the legacy of the character for me as an actor. Selfishly. But it wasn’t the same experience for everybody else and reasonably so. They want to keep working, and it’s a jackpot job. Nobody wants to look for another job. So I felt for everybody. Zoe Perry: But that Zoom afforded Lance and I a chance to express some gratitude to the guys for what we got to participate in all those years. The Armitages took the news as well as you could expect, given that Lee already had a heads-up. But like many people who often turn to humor in uncomfortable situations, Iain attempted to make a few jokes, while Holly Revord remained totally silent. Only at the end did Raegan say, “Sorry, guys, I’m still totally in shock.” Still, the 15-minute Zoom ended on an inspired note, with Osment saying she was going to start making baked goods for everyone to celebrate the final episodes, and Lee Armitage offering up a virtual group hug to everyone. “We’ll see you in a couple weeks,” Lorre said, followed by several “Love you’s” among the cast. Of course, it wasn’t until after everyone logged off that the weight of what just happened started to feel real. Iain Armitage in Young Sheldon . CBS/2024 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. Holly Revord: Raegan just went to their room and cried. I wish that the producers would have given the moms, at least, a heads-up about how to handle it with our kids. I mean, the kids spent half their life on that show. They don’t know another world. Lance Barber: I think we all got together on a call right after with each other [since] the reveal of the news felt informal and impersonal over Zoom. It gave them a buffer of us not being able to come up to them afterward and saying, “What the fuck?” But I realize now, which I hadn’t thought of at the time, that they wanted to tell us right away instead of waiting any longer, and not everyone was back in town yet. Holly Revord: But when we were told it was “a creative decision,” it just felt like bullshit, and something we were being fed. There’s obviously still storylines. The Cooper family is still around a lot. Just on a different show. Annie Potts: I can’t remember what happened after that Zoom. I think I blacked out. I’m kidding. I think it ended with “Thanks so much for the last seven years!” I mean, you couldn’t have just done that for one more year? But I had heard some people saying in season six, “I don’t know, this could be our last year because the kids are grown up now, and he’s going off to Pasadena.” And it was like, “Well, let him go! Let him go to Pasadena!” [ Laughs ] I think the audience would have been fine with letting him go off to Pasadena and hanging with the rest of us. But it wasn’t my call. Connor Kilpatrick: We knew something was happening that day because all the executives showed up at our office building. And when you go to the office and there’s a bunch of fancy cars that are not normally there, and everybody is dressed nicer than normal, we know something’s going on. They had a meeting all morning, we started late, then they were in their offices for a while, locked behind closed doors. Right after they told the cast, the Steves finally came into the writers room and told us, and then they had a bunch of phone calls to make. And I went into my office and cried for 30 minutes. Even when I was told the writers room was regathering, I was like, “I can’t, I’m not ready. I can’t go back in there.” And even when I did, there were still tears in my eyes. It was a hard day. Chuck Lorre: It was heartbreaking. There’s no way around it. One thing about a television show that succeeds is that a family is created over many years, and when you bring it to an end, there’s grieving. But unlike a movie where you work together on an intense experience for two to four months … a television series, if you’re lucky, goes on for years. And it’s very hard to say goodbye. A press release announcing the end of the show was released immediately. Lorre, Molaro and Holland thanked the fans, while CBS president Amy Reisenbach added, “ Young Sheldon proved lightning can strike twice. It set itself apart with a remarkable cast that felt like a family from the first moment we saw them onscreen and brought characters to life with unique heartfelt stories that drew audiences in from the start. We extend a sincere thank you to executive producers Chuck Lorre, Steve Molaro and Steve Holland and the entire writing and producing teams for six wonderful seasons. We look forward to seeing their final season unfold and giving it a proper send off with the best episodes yet for their fans to enjoy.” Not included in the press release was the news that CBS was going to greenlight a spin-off focused on the characters of Georgie and Mandy. And that’s where things got really messy. *** Excerpted from Young Sheldon Copyright © 2026 Jessica Radloff. Published by Grand Central Publishing, a Hachette Book Group company. title: Steven Spielberg to Oversee ‘Transformers’ Franchise With Eighth Movie in the Works at Paramount Pictures

Jordan 4 days ago See All John Nacion/Variety Steven Spielberg has taken on the task of helming the “ Transformers ” franchise amid development on Paramount Pictures’ eighth movie based on the IP. He will serve as an executive producer on “Transformers 8,” as he has on previous “Transformers” films, but also oversee all creative aspects of the live-action film working alongside Lorenzo di Bonaventura, insiders tell Variety . The intention is for Spielberg and di Bonaventura to produce a film with a similar tone to the earlier “Transformers” movies, which Spielberg had more involvement with. Spielberg collaborated on the first two “Transformers” films in a similar capacity. The new movie is being written by Jason Fuchs. title: László Nemes Boards Jack The Ripper Series ‘Sickert’ (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All October 6, 2026 8:00am László Nemes and producer Alexander Rodnyansky Neilson Barnard/Getty Images; Aldara Zarraoa/Getty Images László Nemes , the Oscar-winning director of Son of Saul , is attached to co-write and direct Sickert , a historical thriller series set in the world of Jack the Ripper. The limited series is focused on influential German-British painter and visual artist Walter Sickert, suspected by some historical theorists as being the Victorian serial killer. Adam Baroukh will co-write the series. Oscar-nominated producer Alexander Rodnyansky ( Leviathan , Loveless ) will produce through his AR Content production banner. Nemes will also serve as executive producer alongside Rodnyansky, Stuart Manashil, and Michael Kupisk. Related Stories Movies American French Film Festival Lineup Features Int'l Oscar Contenders, "Cinema of Resistance" Movies London Film Fest Gets Concrete - Literally, and More Than Once! “My fascination for the first modern serial killer and for the mystery of the gothic world of Victorian London dates back to my childhood,” Nemes said in a statement. “I have the ambition to tell a story that is both epic and personal, frightening and illuminating, and to immerse today’s viewer in a universe that remains largely uncharted.” Set in London in 1888, a city gripped by panic over Jack the Ripper’s brutal murders, Sickert follows the artist as he straddles both the world of art and high society, and that of the marginalized underclass Sickert is drawn to paint, the very people Ripper is claiming as victims. When Sickert becomes a person of interest in Scotland Yard’s murder investigation, the artist’s grip on reality begins to falter and he starts doubting his own innocence and identity. Nemes says he will base the style of the Sickert series on historical records as well as from the real artist’s own haunting paintings of life in the ghettos of Whitechapel, where Jack the Ripper found his victims. Walter Sickert’s work is credited with influencing artists like Francis Bacon and Lucien Freud, and the artist was a key figure in avant garde movements including the London Impressionists and the Camden Town Group. Nemes won an Oscar for his debut feature, the Holocaust drama Son of Saul (2015). He followed up with the period dramas Sunset (2018) and Orphan (2025). His latest, Moulin , his first French-language film, depicting the story of French resistance leader Jean Moulin , premiered in Cannes competition this year. AR Content produced Orphan , which premiered in Venice last year. The company’s current slate includes Place to Be from Hungarian director Kornél Mundruczó, starring Ellen Burstyn, Taika Waititi, and Pamela Anderson, and Amos Gitai’s documentary The Road to Jericho , both of which premiered in Venice this year. On the TV side, AR Content produced High Value Target: The Hunt for Saddam , a limited series starring Joel Kinnaman, on TNT. THR

title: Ava DuVernay Returns With One of Netflix’s Most Political Docs Ever: “This Movie Kicked My Butt”
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close Ava DuVernay in 2023. Gioncarlo Valentine/The New York Times/Redux In an early September morning over breakfast on a restaurant patio in her Eastside L.A. neighborhood, Ava DuVernay is remembering a piece of advice Steven Spielberg gave her more than a decade ago. Around the release of Selma , the fiery 2014 historical drama that received a best picture Oscar nomination, DuVernay attended a dinner at J.J. Abrams’ house and found herself seated next to Spielberg. Her movie was launching her into a new sphere of opportunity — and visibility — in Hollywood, and there, a few inches away, was arguably the most famous filmmaker in the world. She marveled to Spielberg, “Your name is on so many things — even things that you don’t direct,” before asking how he handled the pressure of delivering every time. What if a project left his fans or peers disappointed? Related Stories TV Jamie Foxx Does Not Want to Be Canceled Over New Hulu Stand-up Special: "After That Kevin Hart Roast, I Had to Cut Everything" Beyond the Book Zoe Kazan on Honoring Steinbeck's 'East of Eden' for Netflix Series While Rethinking Its Characters “He said, ‘You make another one,’ ” DuVernay recalls. ” ‘You just keep going.’ “ DuVernay has held that advice close ever since. This morning, she’s only a few weeks from the New York Film Festival premiere of her latest film, 14th , a documentary about the 14th Amendment and its increasingly fraught place in American political life. It’s a companion piece to her Oscar-nominated 2016 documentary 13th , which examined mass incarceration and the prison-industrial complex through the amendment that abolished slavery. The new film also comes on the heels of Origin , DuVernay’s ambitious 2023 narrative drama, which resonated with critics but — like even a few Spielberg movies — underperformed with audiences. “I’ve talked to a lot of fellow filmmakers about that experience,” she says. “Some really famous, well-known guy friends reminded me that everyone has films that are not as widely seen as they should be.” And so, on to the next. The director on the set of her 2023 narrative drama Origin . Neon/Courtesy Everett Collection The idea for 14th came to DuVernay in early 2024, when Donald Trump , campaigning to return to the White House, was promising to challenge birthright citizenship — one of the rights enshrined in the 14th Amendment. At first, that gave her the movie’s frame. Then the frame kept widening. Once Trump was back in office, the amendment seemed to keep turning up in the news: due process, public debt, even its language around “insurrection or rebellion.” What had begun as a film about one contested constitutional guarantee was becoming something larger — and, for DuVernay, harder to pin down while history was still moving beneath her feet. “This movie kicked my butt because it was like building a plane midflight — so much stuff was coming in every day, everything was happening,” DuVernay says. During production, she followed Carla Hayden, the first African American and first woman to serve as librarian of Congress; three weeks later, Hayden was fired. She followed Dr. Lonnie Bunch, the first Black secretary of the Smithsonian Institution who later retired amid speculation of political pressure, which Bunch has denied. “All my feelings about everything happening in the past three years — creatively, politically, socially, culturally — are being put into this film,” she says. “At least I’ve felt productive and not like I was going crazy with worry and fear and anger.” For 14th , DuVernay interviewed more than 50 experts, scholars and politicians, interweaving their insights with vérité interludes and brief snippets of relevant stand-up from comedians like Hasan Minhaj. “Comedians are the last frontier of truth-telling,” she says. The film was made for Netflix , which DuVernay considers her “home studio,” having worked with the Ted Sarandos- and Greg Peters-run streamer on such projects as 13th . But 14th arrives as some of Hollywood’s largest companies have come under scrutiny for their handling of politically sensitive material. Amazon dropped the Sam Altman docudrama Artificial with the statement, “We believe that Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio,” after striking a major deal with Altman’s OpenAI. (Neon quickly picked it up.) Apple, meanwhile, pushed the Jessica Chastain political-violence thriller The Savant by more than a year after the assassination of Charlie Kirk; Chastain later said she was “not aligned” with that decision. DuVernay interviews activist and philosopher Angela Davis for 13th. Courtesy of Netflix 14th ranks among the more overtly political projects Netflix has backed, and DuVernay wondered whether the company would stay out of her way. “I was really hopeful that they would continue to support the filmmakers in the way that they’ve established — and they did,” she says. “I was hoping they would hold their stance under what has felt like a lot of pressure to do otherwise. … In this climate, I would’ve expected a little more ‘helicopter mom.’ ” The cancellation of Stephen Colbert’s late night show, the turmoil around Jimmy Kimmel and Paramount’s settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against 60 Minutes all registered with DuVernay as she worked. Most unnerving was the short-lived merger agreement between Warner Bros. Discovery and Netflix, which drew attention in Washington. “I was like, ‘What’s this merger? What’s happening? What’s going on?’ ” DuVernay recalls asking Adam Del Deo, Netflix’s vp docs. “He said, ‘Ava, just keep making the movie you want to make. I can’t tell you what’s going to happen. I really don’t know what’s happening.’ “ She then asked, “Are you guys going to drop this?” Del Deo responded, “I don’t know. Just keep making it.” “I feel like everyone’s afraid, and I’m no exception — I’ve been cautioned about this material and about my points of view on all kinds of things,” DuVernay says. “We’ve seen a total recession in films by certain kinds of people and movies made for certain amounts of money — I think artists and executives feel a lot less free.” A former film publicist, DuVernay broke out behind the camera in the 2010s with the emotional, character-driven indies I Will Follow and Middle of Nowhere . Since then, she has moved across documentaries, limited series and big studio movies. Her 2018 Disney tentpole A Wrinkle in Time disappointed at the box office; a year later came the massively popular and Emmy-winning When They See Us . Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor stars in the film, based on Isabel Wilkerson’s Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents. Neon/Courtesy Everett Collection Over time, she has grown less interested in being one of the industry’s designated spokespeople on representation. “Is Alex Gibney going to get that question? Is Nathan Fielder going to get that question? What are those directors doing from their position for women?” she asks, referencing the men behind other high-profile documentaries this fall, Musk and You Can See Everything . “Until it’s a priority for everyone who says that they care about other people and are interested in a just world, then there won’t be one. “You’re making a choice for the types of films that you make to look a certain way — you’re making all those choices — and so people will make their choices, and I’ll make mine. My choice is just to try to be self-sustaining,” she continues. “I used to be the poster child of talking about this because I felt like it could make a difference — but what I’ve come to realize is it’s too difficult to do if enough people aren’t on board, and there just aren’t enough people on board. It doesn’t mean give up — it means just do it in other ways.” Her work still continues, for instance, with Array, her sprawling distribution and advocacy company for underrepresented filmmakers. One way 14th differs from 13th is in the audience DuVernay imagined watching it — particularly its attention span and knowledge base. Early in the process, she ran an informal poll of people at the Grove in Los Angeles, asking what they knew about the Civil War, who fought it and what it was about. DuVernay with sitting Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden while making 14th. Paul Garnes/Netflix “The answers were startling, shocking, in terms of people not even having an idea,” she says. “But I don’t want people to feel bad about what they don’t know. I don’t want people to feel overwhelmed.” The film features historians, current and former senators and members of Congress, and political operatives, but DuVernay widened the mix to include commentators with big online followings, among them Ringer podcaster Van Lathan Jr. and Hasan Piker, the left-wing Twitch flamethrower who has become one of the right’s favorite media bogeymen. “I would like people to feel like you can enter into this — that this is not going to feel like medicine,” DuVernay says. Sherrilyn Ifill, former head of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and one of the film’s most prominent legal voices, says DuVernay was unusually good at keeping all that expertise from swallowing the movie. “I was routinely stunned by how quickly she seemed to absorb detailed information,” she says. “Ava never loses sight of her audience. I had to trust her to bring me back from the minutiae and to remember the ordinary people she hopes to reach with the film.” As DuVernay puts it, “I wanted different people to be able to see themselves.” Which at times proved to be difficult. U.S. Rep. Charles Rangel in the Oscar-nominated 2016 doc, which explores the amendment that abolished slavery and its connection to the present-day prison system. Courtesy of Netflix Getting Republicans into the film, for instance, proved a considerable challenge. DuVernay says her team approached nearly 300 GOP officeholders, but only a little more than a dozen engaged with them at all. That group included conservative Trump critics like strategist Steve Schmidt and former Sen. Jeff Flake. Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna did agree to participate and defends Trump administration policies in the documentary. “Although I am diametrically opposed to almost everything she believes, I had a lot of appreciation for Anna Paulina flying into New York and sitting there with me,” DuVernay says. “No one else would. We asked. I have the receipts.” DuVernay insists 14th is not a Trump takedown. “He’s a small cog in a wheel that’s been rolling for a very, very long time,” she says. “The current administration is embracing tactics that are tried-and-true and have been tested and weaponized in new ways.” She thinks of the movie instead as a record — of the history it recounts and the period in which she made it. “COVID, wars, Gaza — it’s been quite a decade, and I don’t think we, as people who experience it, appreciate what we’re living through. They’re going to study this time,” DuVernay says. “My question is, how are we getting our arms around that artistically? This film is like an essay. We were writing through it, about what we discovered, how we felt and what it means.” This story first appeared in the Oct. 7 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: American French Film Festival Lineup Features Int’l Oscar Contenders, “Cinema of Resistance”
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 6, 2026 8:00am 'Minotaur' Mubi The Franco-American Cultural Fund (FACF) has unveiled the full lineup of films and series for the 30th American French Film Festival (TAFFF), which will compete for the TAFFF Awards. The fest, running Nov. 3-8 at the Directors Guild of America (DGA) Theater Complex on Sunset Boulevard, will screen international feature film contenders galore, from Minotaur and Fjord to All of a Sudden . Overall, it will showcase 60 films and series. “Since 1997, the Franco-American Cultural Fund, founder of The American French Film Festival, has brought more than 1,200 French films and series into the Hollywood spotlight and given thousands of French artists, from newcomers to well-known directors, to writers, composers, actors, and producers, the opportunity to present their work before their American peers in the heart of Hollywood,” said director Taylor Hackford, a FACF board member. “This year, there will be another spectacular selection and delegation to celebrate the 30th anniversary event at the Directors Guild of America, making TAFFF the second oldest film festival in the city of Angels.” Related Stories TV László Nemes Boards Jack The Ripper Series 'Sickert' (Exclusive) Movies London Film Fest Gets Concrete - Literally, and More Than Once! François Truffart, executive producer and programmer of the festival since 2004, added: “Supporting filmmakers from their earliest short films to eventual Oscar recognition, creating a platform where both established and emerging talent can present their work, being the first to launch a series competition alongside feature films, and consistently championing female filmmakers are just a few of the many meaningful milestones I cherish with TAFFF.” Anouchka van Riel, TAFFF’s deputy director, described this year’s selection as “a cinema of resistance.” She added: “Individuals stand up to systems that exist to grind them down: a corporate machine in A Good Little Soldier and Minotaur , a courtroom built by men in Women on Trial , an online mob in Forsaken , and an exploitative labor chain in Strawberries . Running alongside that is a quieter thread about care, illness and what we owe one another.” The entire lineup for the 30th anniversary edition of the festival includes 31 fiction features, 11 series, four documentaries and 14 short films, many of which are getting either their North American or U.S. premieres. 58 will be up for The American French Film Festival Awards. Among special events at the fesf are the first U.S. screening of the biopic and box office phenomenon De Gaulle , written and directed by Antonin Baudry, which stars Simon Abkarian as General Charles de Gaulle, the U.S. premiere of the comedy All About Corinne , written and directed by Marc Fitoussi and featuring Isabelle Huppert, the North American premiere of Guillaume Canet’s psychological thriller, Karma , starring Marion Cotillard, and the political thriller Jupiter , written and directed by Alexandre Smia. The list of official submissions for the best international feature film Oscar include France’s entry Minotaur , written and directed by Andrey Zviagintsev, Japan’s All of a Sudden by Ryūsuke Hamaguchi, Belgian submission Coward by Lucas Dhont, Romania’s Fjord , the winner of the Cannes Palme d’Or, written and directed by Cristian Mungiu, and Morroco’s Strawberries by Laïla Marrakchi. The TAFFF program will also highlight French animation with three features: opening film In Waves by Phuong Mai Nguyen, Iron Boy , written and directed by Louis Clichy, and Blaise by Dimitri Planchon and Jean-Paul Guigue. With the festival moving from spring to fall, TAFFF is this year also bringing the best French films from Cannes, Venice and Locarno to Hollywood, including Gentle Monster , written and directed by Marie Kreuzer and starring Léa Seydoux, One Minute to Midnight by Nicolas Pariser, The Green Eyes , written and directed by Fanny Liatard and Jeremy Trouilh. Seven films will compete for the best first feature at TAFFF this year, including Congo Boy , written and directed by Rafiki Fariala, and Cannes Critics’ Week winner La Gradiva , written and directed by Marine Atlan. title: Music Industry Moves: Thomas Rhett Strikes Label Partnership With Hybe’s Blue Highway Records
